title: 报道：Silver Lake 与沙特 PIF 就收购 Unity 展开洽谈

Silver Lake and the Saudi Arabia PIF explore Unity acquisition
Business
Console
PC
Mobile
News
Report: Silver Lake and the Saudi Arabia PIF hold talks with Unity to explore acquisition
The investment partners recently acquired Electronic Arts and are now reportedly turning their gaze toward software engine Unity.
Imran Khan
,
Contributing Editor
,
GameDeveloper.com
November 6, 2026
schedule
2 Min Read
via Unity
Unity Software, the company behind the Unity game engine, is in conversations with Silver Lake and the Saudi Arabia Private Investment Fund,
according to new reporting from Reuters
. Both Silver Lake and the PIF just recently finalized an acquisition of Electronic Arts, taking the company private in a leveraged buyout.
The Reuters story states that a consortium of investors are involved, with the biggest being Silver Lake—owned by United States President Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner—and Saudi Arabia's Private Investment Fund, which has
been investing
in numerous
video game and technology companies
internationally. Silver Lake already owns eight percent of Unity, but Reuters reports that PIF approached both Unity and the investment firm to make an offer for a full buyout.
The sources for the Reuters report also state that the deal would take the form of a leveraged buyout,
much like the Electronic Arts deal
which purchased the company with funds that would need to be recouped by its operating profit. While not being the record-breaking numbers the EA acquisition boasted, this would still be one of the biggest leveraged buyouts in history.
Related:
Nintendo confident in memory supply in new financial report
Unity's game engine is used, by their own accounting, in over half of all mobile games and a large proportion of console and PC games. Scopely, which is already owned by the PIF and Silver Lake among others, uses it to power titles like
Pokémon Go
and
Monopoly Go
.
Unity has expanded to an AI-prominent structure, recently launching
a prompt-based tool in collaboration with Google
to create games entirely from user prompts called Unity Spark.
The company unveiled a new policy of Runtime Fees in 2024 which was intended to charge developers a per-install tariff, but a monumental backlash to the idea from developers
forced Unity to undo the planned policy
. Declining stock prices were perhaps the reason then-Unity CEO John Riccitiello—also former CEO of Electronic Arts—resigned from his position. The current CEO, Matthew Bromberg, was also a former EA executive who acted as General Manager of BioWare, a studio
which the publisher recently shut down
as it attempts to pay off the leveraged buyout from Silver Lake and PIF.
The backlash that unseated Riccitiello shows that Unity is not inured to revolt from its client-facing business, unlike Electronic Arts which does not deal directly with individual developers at a similar scale. A buyout from new,
controversial
owners could lead to an upheaval in Unity's core business, potentially putting the company's operating profit at risk.
